source.title: Interpreting Deep Visual Representations via Network Dissection
source.authors: Bo-Lei Zhou; David Bau; A. Oliva; A. Torralba

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures visual-unit interpretability and how it varies across architectures and training conditions, using Broden alignment and unique-detector counts rather than the claim’s language-model pole audit.
record.gate_note: The paper reports network-dissection results relevant to V4: architecture comparisons, regularization variants, and width changes. Results in figures are recorded as figure only where the text does not give per-model numbers. The human-rating validation, rotation experiment, self-supervised-task comparisons, and transfer-learning results do not directly test the architecture/regularization/tool claim in V4 and are not included as rows. The prediction-explanation examples use interpreted units but do not test attribution graphs or reconstruction error. Statements cited from prior work are excluded.
record.test_reason: Network Dissection counts unit–concept detectors in vision CNNs across architectures, regularization (dropout, batch norm) and width. This bears on V4's claim that architecture and regularization shape how interpretable units are. It does not use the essay's pole audit or the InceptionV1 estimates.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors find units significantly more interpretable than a random rotated basis of equal discriminative power. They also caution that batch normalization can destroy interpretability, so interpretability must be measured separately from accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CNN unit activation maps and IoU alignment against densely labeled visual concepts in Broden; it does not use language-model-generated explanations or simulate neuron activations on held-out text.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability varies with architecture, training dataset, dropout, batch normalization, layer width, and the activation threshold used for unit segmentation.

fits_no_version.finding: Interpretability is axis-aligned: random rotation cuts unique detectors by about 80% with no loss of discriminative power.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpretable single units reflect a privileged basis, not a generic property of representation directions.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-supervised AlexNets yield mostly texture detectors and few object detectors compared with supervised training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training objective strongly shapes how interpretable units are, independent of architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
record.problems: The paper notes that Broden vocabulary omissions can hide interpretable units, single-unit alignment cannot detect concepts jointly represented by groups of units, activation-map upsampling can misalign units, and the unique-detector count may favor larger networks. The results are visual-concept alignment measures, not direct percentages of all neurons with one job; several relevant per-model values are shown only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported measurements—including human-rating validation (Table 3), random rotations (Figs. 6–8), self-supervised task comparisons (Figs. 12, 14–15), training snapshots and transfer learning (Figs. 18–23), and prediction explanations (Fig. 27)—were not extracted because they do not directly test V4's architecture/regularization/tool claim. The paper does not test the remaining claim versions.

untested.parts: Whether better explanation tools raise the interpretable share; the essay's InceptionV1 estimates of about 5% to 99%; modern non-CNN architectures; any test that messy late-layer neurons are caused by these factors rather than capacity.
No language models, MoE, or trillion-scale models.
No InceptionV1 cat/car neuron or pose analysis.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.
No test of activating-example explanations against held-out firing.

missing.what: Ratio of unique detectors per architecture: VGG highest, not ResNet.
Human-rated interpretable unit shares per AlexNet layer (e.g. conv5 194/256) compared with Network Dissection label agreement. This is a share measure and a comparison of tools.
Dependence on the activation threshold τ: looser thresholds shift labels toward colors and textures. The authors say relative orderings are stable across IoU thresholds.

record.verdict_notes: The measure is unique-concept count on the Broden vocabulary, not a share of units with one job, and the authors flag that it favors larger networks. Several per-model values exist only in figures. Width results bear on capacity as well as architecture.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit, neuron poles, or single-job/two-job/ununderstood shares.
No language models, dense-versus-MoE comparison, or scaling to trillion-parameter networks.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose interpretation, or recursive-generalization account.

The study compares visual CNN architectures and some training conditions, but does not compare explanation tools or test whether better tools raise the share of interpretable units. It does not test the essay’s InceptionV1 estimates of about 5% to about 99%, or establish that architecture, regularization, and weak tools cause messy late-layer units.
No attribution graphs, large language model, reconstruction-error comparison, or test that such graphs explain behavior without a trained replacement model.
No explanation-fit-on-activating-examples test of predictions on separate text or other held-out inputs.
No automated language-model explanation scoring by simulating neuron activations on new text.

source_check.notes: All architecture values are figure-only rankings, and the text gives one ordering for ImageNet and Places together. Not in rows: Table 3 human-validated interpretable units (AlexNet conv5 194/256), and Sec. 3.2 rotation (80% fewer unique detectors in a rotated basis). Fig. 11 shows GoogLeNet units on 'concept generalizations' (horses and dogs), which is qualitative and possibly relevant to V3.

statements.correction: Sec. 3.8: the plateau may reflect a capacity limit of AlexNet, or a limit on how many disentangled concepts help scene classification.
statements.problem: Minor: the authors also give a non-capacity explanation for the plateau, and the statement leaves it out. This study's own verdict is limits_scope; the 'challenges' tag belongs to SemanticLens.

statements.correction: GoogLeNet appears in Fig. 9 (count, and ratio of unique detectors per unit), Fig. 13 (layer-wise count and ratio, Places365), Fig. 11 (detector examples) and Fig. 26 (unique object detectors vs accuracy). The text states no numeric share or ratio for GoogLeNet.
statements.problem: GoogLeNet appears in more than the count ranking. Fig. 9's lower plot and Fig. 13 plot its per-unit ratio of unique detectors, which is share-like but given only in figures.

statements.correction: 1711.05611 Table 3 (Sec. 3.1, AlexNet; baseline human descriptions from [1]): interpretable units conv1 57/96, conv2 126/256, conv3 247/384, conv4 258/384, conv5 194/256. Not in rows.
statements.problem: The statement says share-like numbers appear only in four other studies. This study's Table 3 gives human-validated interpretable-unit fractions per AlexNet layer, a parallel to the 1811.10597 '154 of 201' figure.

statements.correction: Discussion, Fig. 28 (AlexNet conv5, Places205, tau 0.0025 to 0.04): a larger tau, or no threshold, gives more color, texture and large-region labels. A tau below 0.005 finds fewer objects. Sec. 2.2: different IoU thresholds change detector counts, but relative orderings remain stable.
statements.problem: The paper states that relative orderings stay stable for the IoU detector threshold (>0.04), not for the activation threshold tau. The color/texture shift happens only with larger tau.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Architecture comparisons on ImageNet and Places
reader_labels.reason: The study explicitly ranks unique-detector counts as ResNet > DenseNet > VGG > GoogLeNet > AlexNet, supporting an architecture-related difference in the tested visual CNNs (r1-r10).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Removing dropout shifts detector categories in opposite directions, batch normalization significantly decreases interpretability, and further widening to 1024 or 2048 units does not significantly increase unique concepts (r11-r13, r16-r17).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: AlexNet widened to 768 conv5 units or widened across convolutional layers
reader_labels.reason: The wide AlexNet variants have many more unique concept detectors while retaining similar classification accuracy to standard AlexNet (r14-r15).
